plan.contextChunk: This figure is a perspective line drawing of a rectangular coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field. The coil appears as a tall rectangular loop of several stacked turns, rendered as a striped gray band so the windings show, and tilted so its face is seen obliquely. A vertical axis labeled z passes through the coil's center, solid above and below the loop and dashed where it crosses the interior; a small circular arrow curls around its top to give the sense of rotation. A second axis labeled x runs diagonally toward the lower left, with a dashed segment continuing to the upper right. From the center point, a bold blue arrow labeled B points horizontally to the right as the uniform field, while an orange arrow labeled n-hat, the unit normal to the coil's surface, springs from the same origin and tilts down and to the right; a thin arc between the two marks the angle theta. Anchoring n-hat and B at a shared origin makes the angle between them the one quantity the reader tracks as the loop turns. The arrangement sets up the flux through a rotating coil and the emf that rotation induces.

elements: vertical z-axis: solid line above and below the coil, dashed segment where it crosses the coil interior, arrowhead and label 'z' at top
small circular rotation arrow curling around the top of the z-axis indicating spin direction
x-axis running diagonally toward lower-left (solid) with a dashed continuation to the upper-right, arrowhead and label 'x' at the lower-left end
rectangular multi-turn coil: a tall rectangle (several nested/stacked turns drawn as a striped gray band) centered on the origin, its plane perpendicular to n-hat and tall along z
blue uniform-field vector B: bold arrow from the origin pointing horizontally to screen-right, label 'B' at its tip
orange unit-normal vector n-hat: bold arrow from the same origin, perpendicular to the coil face, label 'n' with a hat
thin black arc between B and n-hat marking the angle, label 'theta'
shared origin point where the axes, B and n-hat meet
(graph view) time axis t and value axis, blue flux curve Phi = BA cos(theta), orange emf curve epsilon = BA*omega sin(theta), a moving time marker dot, legend labels Phi and epsilon

interactions.label: Coil angle theta
interactions.teaches: Rotating the loop about the z-axis sweeps n-hat relative to the fixed B; the flux readout BA cos(theta) falls to zero when the coil is edge-on, showing only the field component piercing the coil area contributes to magnetic flux

interactions.label: Steady rotation
interactions.teaches: Playing the spin advances theta = omega*t continuously; the flux and induced-emf traces oscillate in quadrature, making clear that the alternating emf arises from the time-changing angle between n-hat and B

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching from the 3D coil diagram to the synchronized flux/emf curves connects the geometric angle theta in the picture to the sinusoidal Phi = BA cos(theta) and epsilon = BA*omega sin(theta) used in the calculation

demo_steps.title: Field-aligned (max flux)
demo_steps.narration: At theta = 0 the coil normal n-hat points along B, so the full field threads the loop and flux = BA is maximal; emf is momentarily zero.

demo_steps.title: Tilted coil
demo_steps.narration: Drag to theta = 45. n-hat tilts away from B and the flux readout drops to BA cos45 ~ 0.71 BA — only the perpendicular field component counts.

demo_steps.title: Edge-on (zero flux)
demo_steps.narration: At theta = 90 the coil is edge-on to B, n-hat is perpendicular to the field, flux = 0 and the induced emf is at its peak magnitude.

demo_steps.title: Graph view
demo_steps.narration: Switch to Graph to see flux (cosine) and emf (sine) plotted against time; press Steady rotation to watch the marker sweep both curves in quadrature.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: axes span about +/-2.5 units. z-axis vertical (world +Y up on screen via elevation), x-axis diagonal. Coil is a tall rectangle ~2.0 wide (in its face plane) x 3.0 tall (along z) with ~4-5 nested turns drawn as a striped gray band (#9a9a9a edges on #cfcfcf). B is a bold blue arrow (#0077cc) of length ~2.0 along world +X (screen-right). n-hat is a bold orange arrow (#e8912a) of length ~1.4, horizontal in world, = (cos theta, sin theta, 0) rotating about the vertical z; theta is the angle between n-hat and B. Coil plane is perpendicular to n-hat. Flux readout Phi = B*A*cos(theta) with B=A=1 normalized; emf epsilon = B*A*omega*sin(theta). Graph view: t in [0, 4*pi], flux blue cosine, emf orange sine, shared zero line. Colors: axes black, B blue #0077cc, n-hat orange #e8912a, theta arc black, coil gray.
interactionPlan.notes: Group the 3D coil+axes+vectors and the 2D graph into two THREE.Groups; toggle visibility rather than rebuilding. On every theta change (slider or animation frame) rotate the coil mesh about the vertical axis, reorient the n-hat arrow, redraw the theta arc, and update the flux/emf readouts and graph marker. Drive the animation with requestAnimationFrame advancing theta = omega*t (omega ~ 1 rad/s) and wrap at 360. Render vectors as cylinder shaft + cone head; the striped multi-turn coil as several slightly offset rectangle line-loops or a thin extruded band with parallel groove lines to mimic windings.

authoredContext:
A Rectangular Coil Rotating in a Magnetic Field A rectangular coil of area A and N turns is placed in a uniform magnetic field B→=Bj^, as shown in the figure. The coil is rotated about the z-axis through its center at a constant angular velocity ω. Obtain an expression for the induced emf in the coil.

A rectangular coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field.

Figure shows a rectangular coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field.

Strategy According to the diagram, the angle between the perpendicular to the surface (n^) and the magnetic field (B→) is θ. The dot product of B→·n^ simplifies to only the cosθ component of the magnetic field, namely where the magnetic field projects onto the unit area vector n^. The magnitude of the magnetic field and the area of the loop are fixed over time, which makes the integration simplify quickly. The induced emf is written out using Faraday’s law.
